title: The Deir ʿAlla Plaster Text of Balaam Son of Beor — a Fragment Witness: a Modern Transcription of Combination I (Wikimedia Commons)
language: Deir ʿAlla dialect (Northwest Semitic), Aramaic script

license.payload: The inscription (Tell Deir ʿAlla, Jordan; ink on plaster, c. 800 BCE; found 1967) is ancient. The transcription seated here is a modern drawing by the Wikimedia user Disdero, published on Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 4.0; redistributed under the same licence, attributed to its author. The editions (Hoftijzer and van der Kooij, Aramaic Texts from Deir ʿAlla, Leiden: Brill, 1976; Hackett, The Balaam Text from Deir ʿAllā, 1984) are in copyright and are not seated.

scope: What is openly available of the Book of Balaam son of Beor. The text survives only as ink on fragments of fallen wall plaster from a building at Tell Deir ʿAlla in the Jordan valley and found by H. J. Franken's expedition in 1967, joined into two 'combinations'; Combination I names Balaam son of Beor as a seer of the gods and tells of a night vision of the council of the gods, as its editors read it. The fragments are in the Jordan Archaeological Museum, Amman. No public-domain or openly licensed edition or photograph of the plaster was found in this pass: the editions are in copyright, and the photographs published with them are the editors'. The seat is a fragment witness, named as such: a modern transcription of Combination I under an open licence. The plaster in photographs: QUEUED. The discovery is not recent (1967); the Balaam of the inscription is the Balaam of Numbers 22–24, a prophet known outside the Bible.
why_seated: Asked for by name ("the fragments of the book of balaam … if theyre available anywhere"): the oldest book in a West Semitic language to name a prophet the Bible also names, written on a wall, broken, and read again from its pieces. Seated with what can be openly held, and the rest named.
ruling: Lee Sharks, 2026-10-23: "detour for an ea-corpora seating. lets see. whats available of mayan texts? and then i dont think we have much or any deuterocanonical second temple lit - all those apocalypses. and what about the ethiopian canon? and euclid. all in original language or as close to it as possible. what else?" — "and the Egyptian book of the dead" — "and what about the fragments of the book of balaam? i might be miswriting this. recent discovery. if theyre available anywhere." — "yes yes yes to all - what a meal."
